source.versionTitle: Atra-ḫasīs, Tablet III — best-effort reconstruction from named scholarly editions (the Old Babylonian flood tablet)
source.verificationStatus: best-effort-reconstruction-pending-verification. Reconstructed from the standard scholarly editions (Lambert & Millard 1969, the critical edition; George & Al-Rawi 1996 for the Old Babylonian Sippar witnesses; Foster 2005 Before the Muses 3rd ed.). Line-numbering follows Lambert–Millard 1969, which cites Tablet III by column (III i–viii); this file encodes column and line in the refId as ATRA-WOH-III:{col}.{line}. The eBL corpus L.1.1 (ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/1) and SEAL served as a collation aid only (CC BY-NC — not reproduced). The sign-by-sign transliteration is a best-effort reconstruction and is PENDING COLLATION against Lambert–Millard 1969 and eBL L.1.1; per-line sign values may contain reconstruction errors. Tablet III — the Old Babylonian flood tablet of the scribe Ipiq-Aya (Ku-Aya) — is the best-preserved of the three tablets, so it is reconstructed more fully here than the fragmentary Tablets I–II; the sense of each line is well-attested across the cited editions and should match the downstream English faithfully. This draft curates the flood-arc (the reed-wall warning, the boat, the deluge, Nintu's lament, the gods' hunger, the offering, Enlil's rage, Enki's defense, and the population-limit apparatus); some intervening lines are compressed and marked with editorial-selection gap notes.

source.fragmentationNote: Atra-ḫasīs is a three-tablet Old Babylonian epic (c. 1700 BCE), best preserved in the copy of the scribe Ipiq-Aya / Ku-Aya (reign of Ammi-ṣaduqa). Tablet III is the flood tablet: after Enlil's earlier attempts to reduce humankind (plague, drought, famine — Tablet I end and Tablet II) fail, the council decrees the Flood (abūbu). Tablet III opens with Enki (Ea), oath-bound not to warn a human directly, addressing the reed wall (igāru / kikkišu) of Atra-ḫasīs's hut so that the man overhears: dismantle the house, build a boat (eleppu) roofed like the Apsû and sealed with pitch (kupru), abandon possessions, and keep life (napištu) alive. Atra-ḫasīs loads his family and living creatures; Adad's storm and the seven-day, seven-night Flood destroy humankind; Enki's own heart breaks; the birth-goddess Nintu / Bēlet-ilī / Mami wails for her offspring, who 'fill the river like dragonflies'; the gods, cut off from human offerings, hunger and thirst. When the Flood recedes, Atra-ḫasīs offers a sacrifice, and the starved gods gather over it 'like flies.' Enlil arrives enraged that a human survived; Enki confesses and defends his stratagem, urging measured checks in place of another total flood. Nintu then establishes permanent limits on human fertility — non-bearing women (lā ālittu), the infant-snatching pašittu-demon, and celibate priestess classes (ugbabtu, entu, igiṣītu) under a birth-taboo — together with settled mortality (mūtu), so that the clamor of humankind never again grows unbearable. This is the Mesopotamian flood-narrative in its oldest connected form, the direct antecedent of Gilgamesh XI and a comparandum to Genesis 6–9. This source file reconstructs the flood-arc; intervening spans not reconstructed here are flagged with editorial-selection gap notes in each segment.

notes: *igāru* 'wall.' Enki addresses the reed wall of the hut, not Atra-ḫasīs directly — the loophole by which he keeps the divine oath (mamītu) while the man overhears. See editorial question on the reed-wall address.
*kikkišu* 'reed-fence, reed hut wall'; parallels Gilgamesh XI:21 *kikkiš kikkiš igār igār*.
*eleppa binī* 'build a boat' — the *eleppu*. See editorial question on the flood-vessel term.
*makkūra zērma napišta bulliṭ* — 'reject property and keep *napištu* (life) alive.' See editorial question on *napištu* 'save life.'

*mūtu* 'death' — the settling of permanent mortality on humankind. Etiological: humans, once potentially long-lived, are henceforth mortal so their numbers (and clamor) never again grow unbearable. See editorial question on the mortality close.
Sense well-attested across the cited editions (Lambert–Millard 1969; Foster 2005); sign values are a best-effort reconstruction pending collation.

*ālittu* 'the bearing (woman)' vs *lā ālittu* 'the non-bearing (woman)' — the first permanent check: a class of women who do not give birth. Uncovered by the glossary; see editorial question on the population-limit apparatus.
*pašittu* — the infant-snatching demoness who causes the death of newborns (later identified with Lamaštu). A named agent of infant mortality. Uncovered; see editorial question.
*šerru* 'infant, suckling'; the pašittu seizes the newborn from the mother's lap — an aetiology of infant death.
Three classes of cultic women — *ugbabtu*, *entu*, *(e)giṣītu* — who are sexually restricted, and so do not bear children. Uncovered; see editorial question.
*ikkibu* 'taboo, forbidden thing'; the celibate priestess-classes are placed under a birth-taboo, permanently reducing the birth-rate — the etiological purpose of the whole apparatus.
